questions.stem: Which tissue transports manufactured food from the leaves to other parts of a plant?
questions.explanation: Phloem sieve tubes translocate sucrose and amino acids from the leaves, where they are made, to growing points, fruits and storage organs. Because the destination may be above or below the leaf, phloem transport can go in either direction.

distractorRationale.a: Xylem carries water and mineral salts upwards only
distractorRationale.c: Cambium is a layer of dividing cells that produces new xylem and phloem
distractorRationale.d: The epidermis is a protective surface layer

questions.stem: Water enters a root hair cell from the soil by
questions.explanation: Soil water is more dilute than the cell sap of the root hair, so it has a higher water potential and water crosses the partially permeable membrane by osmosis. No energy is required. Mineral salts, in contrast, are usually taken in by active transport.

distractorRationale.a: Active transport is used for mineral ions, which must move against their gradient
distractorRationale.c: Transpiration is water loss from the leaves, at the other end of the plant
distractorRationale.d: Translocation is the movement of food in the phloem

questions.stem: The main force responsible for lifting water from the roots to the leaves of a tall tree is

options.text: transpiration pull created by evaporation from the leaves
the pumping action of the phloem
active transport by the xylem cells

questions.explanation: Evaporation from the mesophyll removes water from the top of the xylem column, putting the whole column under tension. Because water molecules cohere strongly to one another and adhere to the vessel walls, the column does not break and water is drawn up. Root pressure and capillarity help but cannot account for heights of thirty metres.

distractorRationale.a: Root pressure is too weak to raise water more than a few metres
distractorRationale.c: Phloem carries food and has no pumping action on water
distractorRationale.d: Xylem vessels are dead and hollow, so they cannot carry out active transport

questions.stem: Under which set of conditions would the rate of transpiration be highest?
questions.explanation: Heat gives water molecules more energy to evaporate, dry air keeps the vapour gradient between leaf and atmosphere steep, and wind removes the saturated layer of air at the leaf surface. All three factors act in the same direction, so transpiration is fastest.

distractorRationale.a: All three conditions here slow evaporation and diffusion
distractorRationale.c: Humid air already holds much vapour, so the diffusion gradient is shallow
distractorRationale.d: Dry air helps, but the low temperature and lack of wind hold the rate down

questions.stem: Two identical leafy shoots stand in water. Petroleum jelly is smeared on the lower surface of every leaf of shoot B only. After three hours shoot A has absorbed 4 cm³ of water and shoot B only 1 cm³. The best conclusion is that

options.text: most transpiration occurs through the stomata, which are mainly on the lower surface
water is absorbed only through the leaves
the cuticle is the main route of water loss

questions.explanation: Water uptake replaces water lost, so uptake measures transpiration. Blocking only the lower surface cut the loss to a quarter, which shows both that stomata are the main exit route and that most of them lie on the lower surface.

distractorRationale.a: Petroleum jelly is inert; it blocks pores rather than killing cells
distractorRationale.c: Water was absorbed by the cut stem through the xylem, not through the leaves
distractorRationale.d: If the cuticle were the main route, blocking the stomata would have changed little

questions.stem: Xylem vessels are particularly suited to water transport because they are

options.text: dead, hollow tubes with lignified walls and no end walls
short cells with sieve plates between them
surrounded by companion cells that supply energy

questions.explanation: Because the cells die and their contents and end walls disappear, the vessel becomes a continuous open pipe offering almost no resistance to flow. The lignin in the wall stops the vessel collapsing under the tension of the transpiration pull and also supports the stem.

distractorRationale.a: Cytoplasm would obstruct the flow of water
distractorRationale.c: Sieve plates are a feature of phloem sieve tubes
distractorRationale.d: Companion cells belong to the phloem, where transport is active

questions.stem: A complete ring of bark is removed from around the trunk of an orange tree. Over the following weeks the trunk swells just above the ring and the tree later dies. This shows that

options.text: phloem, which lies in the bark, carries manufactured food downwards to the roots
water can no longer reach the leaves

questions.explanation: Removing the bark removes the phloem but leaves the xylem, which lies deeper, intact. Sugar travelling down from the leaves accumulates above the gap and causes the swelling, while the roots below are cut off from their food supply and eventually starve.

distractorRationale.a: Xylem was not removed, and it carries water upwards, not food downwards
distractorRationale.c: Water continues to reach the leaves because the xylem is undamaged, which is why the tree survives for weeks
distractorRationale.d: Bark contains no chlorophyll and does not photosynthesise

questions.stem: Transpiration in most plants slows down at night because the stomata close.
questions.explanation: True. Guard cells lose turgor in darkness and the stomatal pores close, so the main exit route for water vapour is shut. The cooler night temperature reduces evaporation further, and only a little water escapes slowly through the cuticle.

questions.stem: Which feature of a root hair cell most increases the rate at which it absorbs water?

options.text: Its long, narrow shape, which gives a large surface area

questions.explanation: A root hair is a slender extension of a single epidermal cell that pushes between soil particles, so a huge area of membrane is in contact with the soil water film. A larger surface area means a proportionally faster rate of osmosis.

distractorRationale.b: Root hair walls are thin and permeable; lignin would obstruct water entry
distractorRationale.c: No light reaches the soil, so root hair cells have no chloroplasts
distractorRationale.d: An impermeable cell could not absorb water at all

questions.stem: State four differences between xylem and phloem, and describe the path taken by a water molecule from the soil until it leaves the leaf as vapour.
markingGuide: Any four differences, one mark each: substance carried (water and salts versus sucrose and amino acids); direction (upwards only versus both directions); cells dead versus living; walls lignified versus unlignified; energy not required versus required; additional support function present versus absent
Path step 1: soil water enters the root hair cell by osmosis because the cell sap has a lower water potential (1 mark)
Path step 2: water moves across the cortex from cell to cell by osmosis, down a water potential gradient, into the xylem of the root (2 marks)
Path step 3: water rises up the xylem of root, stem and leaf as a continuous column held together by cohesion and adhesion (2 marks)
Path step 4: water passes into the mesophyll cells, evaporates into the intercellular air spaces and diffuses out through the stomata as vapour (2 marks)
Correct identification of transpiration pull as the force maintaining the flow (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The four differences are best written as matched pairs. The path must run soil, root hair, cortex, root xylem, stem xylem, leaf xylem, mesophyll, air spaces, stomata, and should name osmosis for entry into the root and transpiration pull as the force that maintains the upward flow.
